Part III of the Constitution sets out the Fundamental Rights. For this Part, “the State” includes the Government and Parliament of India, the Government and Legislature of each State, and all local or other authorities within the territory of India or under the control of the Government of India (Article 12). The State shall not make any law that takes away or abridges the rights conferred by Part III; any law made in contravention is void to the extent of the contravention (Article 13(2)).

The rights are organized under several heads. The Right to Equality includes equality before law (Article 14), prohibition of discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth (Article 15), equality of opportunity in matters of public employment (Article 16), abolition of untouchability (Article 17), and abolition of titles (Article 18).

The Right to Freedom includes protection of certain freedoms under Article 19. All citizens have the right to freedom of speech and expression; to assemble peaceably and without arms; to form associations or unions or co-operative societies; to move freely throughout the territory of India; to reside and settle in any part of the territory of India; and to practise any profession, or to carry on any occupation, trade or business. It also includes protection in respect of conviction for offences (Article 20), protection of life and personal liberty—no person shall be deprived of life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law (Article 21), the right to education—free and compulsory education for all children aged six to fourteen years in such manner as the State may by law determine (Article 21A), and protection against arrest and detention in certain cases (Article 22).

The Right against Exploitation prohibits traffic in human beings and forced labour (Article 23) and prohibits employment of children in factories and similar settings (Article 24). The Right to Freedom of Religion includes freedom of conscience and the free profession, practice and propagation of religion (Article 25), freedom to manage religious affairs (Article 26), freedom as to payment of taxes for promotion of any particular religion (Article 27), and freedom as to attendance at religious instruction or worship in certain educational institutions (Article 28). Cultural and Educational Rights protect the interests of minorities (Article 29) and the right of minorities to establish and administer educational institutions (Article 30).

Certain laws are saved: Article 31 on compulsory acquisition of property is omitted, while Articles 31A, 31B and 31C save laws providing for acquisition of estates and related matters, validate certain Acts and Regulations, and save laws giving effect to certain directive principles. Article 31D, concerning anti-national activities, is omitted. The Ninth Schedule is linked to Article 31B and includes, among others, land reform and tenure abolition laws such as the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950; the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948; the Uttar Pradesh Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950; and the Hyderabad Jagirs regulations.

The Right to Constitutional Remedies is guaranteed by Article 32: the right to move the Supreme Court by appropriate proceedings for enforcement of the rights conferred by Part III is guaranteed.

text:
In India, **Fundamental Rights** are the basic rights protected by **Part III of the Constitution**. The State cannot make a law that takes away or abridges these rights; if it does, that law is void to the extent of the violation. (Constitution of India Block, section “Fundamental Rights,” para. 1)

The main Fundamental Rights are:

1. **Right to Equality** — includes equality before law, prohibition of discrimination on grounds such as religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth, equality of opportunity in public employment, abolition of untouchability, and abolition of titles. (Constitution of India Block, section “Fundamental Rights,” para. 2)

2. **Right to Freedom** — includes citizens’ freedoms of speech and expression, peaceful assembly, forming associations/unions/co-operative societies, moving freely in India, residing and settling anywhere in India, and practising any profession or carrying on any occupation, trade or business. It also includes protections relating to criminal conviction, life and personal liberty, education for children aged 6–14, and arrest/detention. (Constitution of India Block, section “Fundamental Rights,” para. 3)

3. **Right against Exploitation** — prohibits trafficking in human beings, forced labour, and employment of children in factories and similar settings. (Constitution of India Block, section “Fundamental Rights,” para. 4)

4. **Right to Freedom of Religion** — includes freedom of conscience and the freedom to profess, practise and propagate religion, manage religious affairs, and protections relating to religious taxes and religious instruction in certain educational institutions. (Constitution of India Block, section “Fundamental Rights,” para. 4)

5. **Cultural and Educational Rights** — protect the interests of minorities and their right to establish and administer educational institutions. (Constitution of India Block, section “Fundamental Rights,” para. 4)

6. **Right to Constitutional Remedies** — allows a person to move the Supreme Court for enforcement of Fundamental Rights under Article 32. (Constitution of India Block, section “Fundamental Rights,” para. 6)

A small clarification: some rights, like the freedoms under Article 19, are specifically stated for **citizens**, while some protections, such as equality before law and life and personal liberty, apply more broadly to “persons” as described in the Constitution.

matches.line: This section introduces the sixth pocket-size diglot edition of the Constitution of India. It explains that the text has been updated to include all amendments up to the Constitution (One Hundred and Sixth Amendment) Act, 2023, with footnotes identifying the Constitution Amendment Acts through which changes were made. Readers should also note the reference materials included in the appendices: Appendix I contains the Constitution (One Hundredth Amendment) Act, 2015, concerning acquired and transferred territories between India and Bangladesh; Appendix II provides the Constitution (Application to Jammu and Kashmir) Order, 2019; and Appendix III provides the declaration under article 370(3) of the Constitution.

This document is the sixth pocket-size diglot edition of the Constitution of India, updated with amendments through the Constitution (One Hundred and Sixth Amendment) Act, 2023, and supplemented by appendices on the India-Bangladesh territories amendment and the constitutional orders concerning Jammu and Kashmir. It sets out India as a sovereign socialist secular democratic republic and a Union of States, describing the powers and composition of the Union, States, Union territories, Parliament, State Legislatures, executive offices, local self-government institutions, and financial and legislative relations. The text details Fundamental Rights, including equality, freedoms, protection of life and liberty, religious and cultural rights, and constitutional remedies before the Supreme Court and High Courts. It also explains the Directive Principles of State Policy as non-justiciable but fundamental guides for governance, and the Fundamental Duties expected of citizens. The Constitution establishes the rule of law by making State action subject to constitutional limits, judicial review, lawful taxation and appropriation, and procedural safeguards in arrest and detention. It describes the judicial system headed by the Supreme Court, with High Courts and subordinate courts, including their jurisdiction, writ powers, appeals, review, transfer of cases, and binding authority of Supreme Court law. The extracts also cover elections, public services, commissions, tribunals, reservations, emergency-related effects on rights, and constitutional mechanisms for maintaining federal governance and accountability.

India, that is Bharat, is a Union of States. Its territory comprises the territories of the States, the Union territories specified in the First Schedule, and any other territories that may be acquired. Parliament may admit or establish new States, and may form new States or alter the areas, boundaries or names of existing States. Laws made for these purposes may amend the First and Fourth Schedules and make supplemental, incidental and consequential provisions, but are not treated as constitutional amendments under article 368.
